html:
The map's label, in 1200, for the Tuareg, Berber-speaking nomads of the central Sahara, shown across the desert from the Hoggar and Aïr mountains to the Niger bend.

The Tuareg herded camels, goats and sheep between desert wells and mountain pastures. They knew the routes across the sand, so they guided, protected or taxed the caravans of the trans-Saharan trade, and sometimes raided them. Society was ranked into noble clans, vassal herders and enslaved workers. Men wore a face veil, and women held property and kept an old Berber script, Tifinagh.

Around this time Tuareg groups were moving south toward the Sahel. Tradition says a Tuareg camp on the Niger grew into Timbuktu. Later they founded the Sultanate of Aïr at Agadez, and dealt, sometimes as subjects and sometimes as rivals, with the Mali and Songhai empires. See also the map's Tuaregs of 900.
